report.answer_text:
The Word of Wisdom didn't become mandatory on a single date. It shifted from advice to a requirement over several decades.
1833: Joseph Smith recorded the revelation, now Doctrine and Covenants 89. It was presented as "not by commandment or constraint" and advised against wine or strong drink, tobacco, and hot drinks (later interpreted as tea and coffee). Many early members, including church leaders, didn't follow it strictly.
Late 1800s: Leaders increasingly urged compliance. Under Joseph F. Smith in the early 1900s, the church promoted it more strongly. This included replacing wine with water in the sacrament.
1908–1919: Some stakes and wards began to require observance for temple recommends. This was inconsistent across the church.
1921: Church president Heber J. Grant made full observance a church-wide standard. It became a firm requirement for temple recommends and a test of full fellowship. This is the date most historians give for when it became effectively mandatory. The timing coincided with Prohibition in the U.S.
Later: The church clarified that the Word of Wisdom also prohibits illegal drugs and the misuse of harmful substances. Observance remains a requirement for temple recommends today.
The 1921 change was about church policy and enforcement, not a rewrite of the scripture. Section 89 itself still says "not by commandment." Church leaders ruled that it was binding by treating it as a commandment in practice.
If you want, I can look up the latest church guidance on what it covers, such as how it treats vaping or caffeinated drinks.
